summary: A guide from Bob Braden to using IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) at UCLA CCN over the network with Telnet. TSO was stable and regularly scheduled but not yet considered production. A user needs a valid charge number and a user ID, and the note says whom to contact.

plainLanguage.summary: A guide to borrowing time on a big computer. You need an account first, and the computer is still being polished, so it is not perfect yet.

subtitle: A guide to accessing IBM TSO at UCLA CCN over the ARPANET.

tldr.problem: Researchers without access to IBM mainframes could not run time-sharing jobs at UCLA CCN.
tldr.mechanism: UCLA made IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) available over the ARPANET using the Telnet protocol. Users needed a valid charge number and TSO user ID from Barbara Noble at UCLA.
tldr.outcome: Network users could now edit files, submit batch jobs, and run programs interactively on the CCN mainframe, though TSO was not yet in production status.

today: RFC 379 is Unknown status. It documents UCLA CCN's TSO installation via Telnet in August 1972, before interactive computing over networks became standard.

sections.title: TSO at CCN
sections.content: UCLA's Computing and Communications Network (CCN) made IBM's Time Sharing Option (TSO) available to network users via Telnet. The system was stable and ran on a regular schedule, though not yet considered production due to restrictions and bugs being fixed. Users needed a valid CCN charge number (billing account) and a TSO user ID. These could be obtained from Barbara Noble at (213) 825-7438 or (213) 825-7452. TSO usage itself was not charged; only batch jobs submitted from TSO were billed to the user's account.
sections.plainLanguage: UCLA opened its mainframe to network users. To use it, you need an account number and a user name, which UCLA hands out. It is still being polished, so it might act oddly.

sections.title: TSO Modes
sections.content: TSO offered two main modes. Conversational Remote Job Entry allowed users to prepare job streams with the EDIT command, SUBMIT them to batch, monitor their STATUS, and retrieve OUTPUT. This was useful for TIP users who wanted to submit any batch job without going through NETRJS on a TENEX machine. Foreground Execution let users run OS/360 programs directly from the terminal, though with limitations: the region was limited to 128K (to be expanded), all referenced datasets must be on resident disk packs, and execution was slow due to time-slicing and swapping. Two important foreground capabilities were the TEST command for DDT-like debugging and the ability for a program to interact with the user's terminal.
sections.plainLanguage: TSO works two ways: you can send a big job to the computer and come back for the answer later, or write a small program and run it right there while you watch.

sections.title: Datasets and Telnet Protocol
sections.content: TSO automatically placed datasets created in the foreground on the right resident disk pack, and all TSO datasets were cataloged by name. At UCLA, dataset names used the charge number and user ID as the highest-order indices, allowing the system to manage a large logical disk. Dataset access was controlled by the charge number: users could read, write or execute any dataset under their charge number, and could rename or scratch such datasets. The RFC noted that programs could not yet open direct network connections. For Telnet access, RFC 377 described how to use the Telnet Network Virtual Terminal to reach TSO, though the current implementation had a bug and lacked full duplex, lowercase input, and proper special character translation.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs store their work on the big disk, organized by who asked for it. The computer is still fixing Telnet so that typing on your terminal works better.

references.text: RFC 377, Using TSO VIA ARPA Network Virtual Terminal
